title: Research and Projects
text: Most of what I work on sits somewhere between mathematics, machine learning, and a real problem someone needs solved. Here are some of the projects I’m proudest of.

title: Research and Projects
text:
Research

Classifying a poultry pathogen from its genome
With Cobb Genetics and the Goswami Lab · Frontiers in Microbiology, 2026
Enterococcus cecorum causes disease in poultry, but plenty of strains are harmless. We asked whether the way genes are arranged around genomic islands could tell the two apart. I engineered 84 genome-level features across 145 genomes and trained random forests with genome-grouped cross-validation so the model couldn’t cheat through near-duplicate samples. It reached an AUROC of 0.918 and beat the simpler baselines. When we held out whole sequencing projects, performance dropped to 0.694, which is an honest reminder that it needs prospective validation before anyone relies on it. Read the paper


Omics and AI for neuronal gene expression
Brain Informatics, 2026
A review that follows computational neuro-omics from co-expression networks to graph neural networks and foundation models, with a focus on Alzheimer’s disease, schizophrenia, and epilepsy. The hard problems turn out to be less about models and more about harmonizing data, aligning spatial measurements, and getting causal interpretations right. Read the review


An algebra for neural networks
Ph.D. work · arXiv, 2024
My dissertation treated neural networks as algebraic objects you can add, compose, and scale, and used that to build networks that approximate solutions to the heat equation with explicit bounds on parameters, depth, and accuracy. Read the preprint


How researchers talk about AI in education
With researchers at Johns Hopkins University · under review
I built an LLM-assisted pipeline that classifies 12,000+ education research abstracts by their sentiment toward AI, using locally deployed models and checking them against human-labeled data. The goal is to see how that sentiment varies across countries and levels of economic development.

title: Research and Projects
text:
Applied projects

Privacy-preserving transaction data with Mastercard
2025 – 2026
Real transaction data can’t go into a classroom. Working with Mastercard data scientists, I used Gaussian mixture models and their differentially private versions to generate synthetic transaction data that keeps the useful structure without exposing anyone. Students then used it for portfolio projects.


Maternal health at Arkansas Blue Cross and Blue Shield
2023
I used difference-in-differences and Granger causality on claims data to study how policy affected maternal-health outcomes, built risk models from claims plus social determinants and Census data, and built an LSTM model that improved claims-volume forecasts by 25%. The results went to stakeholders as R Shiny dashboards.


Children’s nutrition in Birmingham, Alabama
With the UAB Heersink School of Medicine · 2024 – 2025
I analyzed pandemic-era survey data on the nutritional needs of children in underserved Birmingham neighborhoods using factor analysis and structural models. The findings were presented to the Alabama Department of Public Health.


Measuring a digital motivation course
With the Applied Sciences Performance Institute · 2024 – 2025
Together with a psychiatric team, I measured whether an online motivational course actually improved well-being (PERMA), motivation, depression, and anxiety. I compared intervention and control groups with ANOVA, ANCOVA, nonparametric tests, and A/B testing in R, and used the results to recommend which courses worked best for which groups.

title: Research and Projects
text:
Code

nnR
An R package on CRAN that implements the algebraic operations on neural networks from my dissertation. I wanted the math to be something you could run and poke at, not just read. It has full documentation, a vignette, and about 90% test coverage.


RustQC
A reimplementation of core FastQC functionality in Rust for sequencing quality control. Early in-memory benchmarks run more than 40 times faster than FastQC.
More on GitHub.

title: Teaching
text:
I’ve been teaching since 2020, first mathematics and now data science. My goal is simple: help students become effective, hard-working, and ethical data workers.
I try to teach the reasoning before the tools. Students should know what a model assumes and how it can fail before they reach for a library. I also want them to practice the whole job, not just the modeling step: version control, cleaning messy data, testing, deployment, and explaining results to someone who isn’t a data scientist. And I want them to treat privacy, bias, and leakage as part of the engineering, not an afterthought.

title: Teaching
text:
Courses

Generative and Agentic AI
Students build RAG systems, orchestration pipelines, and agentic workflows. We run local LLMs with Ollama, build pipelines with LangChain, and monitor them with LangSmith. I also developed versions of this course and an applied Python course for Arkansas’s statewide data science program, for people looking to upskill or reskill. About 150 students have taken them so far, including about 80 members of the National Guard Reserve. These courses received the inaugural University of Arkansas Global Campus Award for Excellence in Course Design in 2025.


Statistical Learning
I rebuilt this course around how modeling is done today: tidymodels, real data cleaning, and deployment with Docker and MLflow.


Principles of Data Science
An introduction for about 80 incoming freshmen covering the data science process, the tools of the profession, and its ethics.

title: Shakil A. Rafi, Ph.D.
text:
I’m a Teaching Assistant Professor of Data Science at the University of Arkansas, where I teach machine learning and applied AI.
I came to data science through mathematics. My Ph.D. is in applied math, and my dissertation looked at how neural networks approximate solutions to the heat equation: how many parameters they need, how deep they have to be, and how accurate they can get. That habit of asking why a method works still shapes how I build things and how I teach.
After my Ph.D. I spent a year as a postdoc in computational biology, building machine learning models on bacterial genomes. Before that I did health data science at Arkansas Blue Cross and Blue Shield, and taught in the Walton College of Business. Long before any of that, I co-founded a small web development company in Dhaka.
These days most of my time goes to students. I want them to leave my classes as effective, hard-working, and above all ethical data workers. I also work with industry partners like Mastercard, Walmart, Tyson, J.B. Hunt, and Arvest Bank so students get to work on real problems with real data.
